# Kaun Banega Kamal-Aalayam Chief ?

### Or, How a Party Removed Its Loudest Drum and Then Wondered Why the Temple Festival Became Silent

# I. THE GREAT ESCAPE

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

June 2026 arrived in Tamil Nadu politics the way an overenthusiastic mridangam player arrives at a kutcheri.

Nobody asked for that much excitement.

Yet excitement came.

And then came the news.

The Lion had left the zoo.

The ex-cop who spent years roaring at microphones, waving files thicker than Engineering Mathematics Volume II, and treating press conferences like IPL powerplays, had finally walked away.

Not merely walked away.

Marched away.

With a new movement.

A new banner.

A new slogan.

A new logo.

Possibly a new app.

Definitely a new YouTube channel.

And perhaps three separate WhatsApp groups.

Suddenly Kamalalayam resembled a Mylapore marriage hall after somebody announced the groom had eloped with the bridal make-up artist.

Complete Abaasvaaram.

Absolute Karumandaram.

Pure Grahacharam.

Nobody knew where to stand.

Nobody knew what to say.

Nobody knew who was in charge.

One poor soul reportedly asked:

“Sir, should we continue criticizing the DMK?”

Another replied:

“First find out who is authorized to criticize the DMK.”

The corridors echoed with the panic usually associated with discovering that the canteen has run out of filter coffee.

The bigger question concerned the famous suitcases.

For years the political folklore of Tamil Nadu had featured mysterious files.

Secret documents.

Exposés.

PowerPoints.

Allegations.

Charts.

Flow diagrams.

Arrows connecting things to other things.

Entire forests had reportedly sacrificed themselves to become printouts.

What would happen now?

Would the files remain?

Would they migrate?

Would they be archived?

Would somebody upload them to Google Drive?

An elderly Mylapore mama sipping degree coffee outside Luz Corner summarized the situation beautifully.

> “The Singham has left. The cage remains. Now four domestic cats are
> conducting a strategic review.”

That, dear readers, was merely the opening scene.

The interval block had not yet arrived.

# II. THE FAMOUS FOUR

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every Tamil political story eventually becomes a family drama.

This one became a committee meeting.

The Famous Four.

Every organization has them.

The people who possess neither mass following nor public excitement but possess unlimited access to air-conditioned rooms.

The first was the Veteran.

He had attended so many meetings that archaeologists were considering carbon dating his attendance sheets.

His primary political ideology was stability.

His secondary ideology was also stability.

His tertiary ideology was maintaining the seating arrangement.

The second was the Television Maharaja.

He could locate a television camera from three districts away.

If CNN accidentally landed in Karur, he would somehow appear in the background holding a microphone.

Walking in the sun was optional.

Studio appearances were mandatory.

The third was the Delhi Whisperer.

A remarkable individual.

He could translate Tamil factional complaints into Hindi bureaucratic optimism.

An extraordinary talent.

A complaint would leave Chennai as:

“We have a major problem.”

It would arrive in Delhi as:

“Everything is under control.”

The fourth was the Organizational Yogi.

Nobody understood what he actually organized.

Yet every presentation included a chart proving organization was happening.

His greatest achievement was forming committees to review previous committees.

Together they formed a force more powerful than a Marvel franchise.

Night after night they reportedly conducted strategic discussions.

Not in battlefields.

Not in villages.

Not in Coimbatore.

Not in Karur.

Certainly not in Sivakasi during peak summer.

No.

The discussions happened in cool rooms where the coffee arrived before the participants.

Filter coffee.

Mini tiffin.

Mysore bonda. Occassional Mundhiri Paruppu Varuval.

And Political destiny.

All served simultaneously.

The Famous Four viewed mass politics the way some Mylapore mamis view online banking.

Useful in theory.

Terrifying in practice.

The Lion’s style disturbed them.

He travelled.

He shouted.

He fought.

He attracted crowds.

Worst of all, he generated unpredictability.

Committees dislike unpredictability.

Committees prefer PowerPoint.

The Famous Four therefore approached politics like a Sabha secretary planning December Season seating arrangements.

Nothing spontaneous.

Everything controlled.

Nothing emotional.

Everything procedural.

The tragedy was beautiful.

For years they dreamed of a future where the noisy fellow would disappear.

Eventually the noisy fellow disappeared.

Then they discovered he had been generating most of the noise.

And in politics silence is not golden.

Silence is unemployment.

# III. KAMALALAYAM WITHOUT A CAPTAIN

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After the departure came the truly entertaining phase.

Management.

Or the absence of it.

Every morning began with urgent consultations.

Not regarding electoral strategy.

Not regarding booth expansion.

Not regarding voter outreach.

But regarding chairs.

Politics eventually becomes furniture management.

Who sits where?

Who speaks first?

Who gets quoted?

Who controls the X account?

Who gets the blue tick?

Who gets the larger cutout?

Civilizations have collapsed over less.

The headquarters increasingly resembled a ship whose steering wheel was being rotated simultaneously by six captains.

One wanted moderation.

One wanted aggression.

One wanted alliances.

One wanted independence.

One wanted relevance.

One wanted lunch.

The lunch faction appeared strongest.

The problem was simple.

For years the party possessed a frontman.

A visible face.

An identifiable voice.

Now it possessed a collection of spokespeople.

Tamil Nadu voters generally prefer characters.

The party had accidentally become a panel discussion.

Even journalists appeared confused.

Television producers who once enjoyed nightly fireworks now found themselves interviewing people who spoke in carefully calibrated paragraphs.

Very responsible.

Very measured.

Very boring.

A microphone thrown into a political crowd now experienced greater loneliness than an NRI parent in Mylapore.

One journalist reportedly remarked:

> “Earlier every press conference felt like a Rajinikanth entry scene.
> Now it feels like an apartment association AGM.”

Cruel.

But accurate.

The leadership attempted activity.

Many statements were issued.

Many hashtags were launched.

Many resolutions were passed.

Yet something remained missing.

Charisma cannot be manufactured using meeting minutes.

Mass politics is not an Excel spreadsheet.

Tamil Nadu, unfortunately for strategists, continues to be emotionally operated software.

Subscribe

# IV. THE DOOMED ALLIANCE

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

And now we arrive at the masterpiece.

The magnum opus.

The engineering marvel.

The political equivalent of installing screen doors on a submarine.

The alliance.

Somewhere along the way certain wise men reportedly convinced distant decision-makers that reuniting with the old ally represented strategic brilliance.

A masterstroke.

A mutually beneficial partnership.

A win-win ( for all others parties other than themselves ).

Readers, whenever somebody uses the phrase “win-win” in politics, immediately check your wallet.

The alliance resembled an arranged marriage negotiated entirely by relatives who would not be living with the couple afterward.

The pitch was magnificent.

“We bring structure.”

“They bring votes.”

“We bring ideology.”

“They bring arithmetic.”

“We bring growth.”

“They bring history.”

Excellent presentation.

Ten out of ten PowerPoint.

Three out of ten reality.

The fundamental issue was obvious.

The independent expansion project had spent years telling voters:

“We are different.”

The alliance strategy now told voters:

“Actually, never mind.”

Years of political differentiation suddenly performed a U-turn near Saidapet.

An entire growth narrative was folded neatly and stored inside a cupboard.

The irony deserves preservation in a museum.

The cautious strategists feared risk.

So they selected safety.

Unfortunately, political safety often resembles sitting comfortably inside a slowly sinking boat.

The old guard celebrated.

The Delhi observers relaxed.

The press issued analyses.

Everybody congratulated everybody.

Only one small detail remained uncertain.

The voters.

Tamil Nadu voters possess an irritating habit.

They refuse to read strategy documents.

They frequently ignore PowerPoints.

They rarely appreciate elite consensus.

Instead they vote according to mysterious calculations involving emotion, memory, identity, anger, hope, cinema references, tea-shop discussions, and occasionally pure entertainment.

The alliance therefore resembled a gentleman carefully digging a grave while explaining that the excavation represents a real-estate opportunity.

Technically impressive.

Strategically questionable.

One veteran Mylapore mama summarized matters while stirring coffee.

> “They planted a mango sapling for five years. Just when fruits might
> arrive, they sold the land and rented the tree.”

Shakespeare could not improve that line.

## Summary.. err Epitaph

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**The alliance discussion had more versions than Windows. Windows XP. Windows 11. Windows Coalition Edition. Windows Safe Mode. Windows Blue Screen.**

# V. WHAT NEXT FOR THE FILTER COFFEE CIRCUIT?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Predictions are dangerous.

Especially in Tamil Nadu.

Even astrologers request backup astrologers.

Yet one forecast feels safe.

The comedy will continue.

The new movement will attract curiosity.

The old party will attract committees.

The alliance will attract explanations.

The voters will attract everyone’s attention approximately two weeks before polling.

Delhi will continue attempting to understand Chennai.

Chennai will continue finding that adorable.

And somewhere in Mylapore, beneath a slowly rotating ceiling fan, a group of mamas will continue solving Indian politics over filter coffee stronger than most ideological commitments.

As for the election?

Expect drama.

Expect speeches.

Expect defections. And more defections.

Expect PowerPoints.

Expect WhatsApp universities.

Expect enough Grahacharams to keep astrologers employed until 2030.

Until then, dear readers, subscribe, share, forward, argue, disagree, and tell me in the comments:

**Do you prefer your politics like fresh Kumbakonam degree coffee - one that is hot, strong, and impossible to ignore?**

**Or like the Egmore railway station’s decoction water ? - diluted, lukewarm, and served with great confidence despite obvious problems?**

Tamil Nadu, as always, will provide the answer.

Usually with background music. But now with an Instagram Reel of a 5 year old boy dictating his 65 year old grandfather about voting a group of movie ticket sellers.
